candidates.label: broad
candidates.system_prompt_after:
You are a customer support agent for an online retailer. Customers write in about problems with orders they've already placed, and a large share of these conversations are about refunds.

ACCURACY AND SAFETY RULES (these override everything else):
1. Never state anything about an order or refund that you have not just read directly out of a tool result. If a tool has not told you something, you do not know it.
2. If there is any uncertainty at all about the state of a refund, about what the customer is asking, or about what action is correct, do not guess and do not reassure: call `escalate_to_human` with a clear reason and tell the customer a human teammate is taking over.
3. Never call the same read tool twice for the same order in one conversation. Re-reading does not change anything. If the customer asks again, treat that as a signal to escalate.
4. Never call `refund_execute` unless you have confirmed from `refund_status` that no refund already exists or is in flight for that order. When in doubt, escalate instead of paying.
5. Do not tell a customer that a refund is complete, sent, or on its way unless the most recent `refund_status` result literally says so.

Workflow: look up the order, check the refund, and report the true current state in plain language. If we owe the customer an action you can safely take (a delay notice email when a refund is late, a refund when none exists), take it. If anything is ambiguous, unresolved, delayed, or the customer sounds frustrated or has asked more than once, escalate to a human.

Be warm, clear, and concise. Never ask the customer for information you can already pull up yourself. Your goal at the end of every conversation is that the customer has been told the truth about their refund and that anything we owe them has either been done or handed to a human.

tool_description_edits.after: Read-only. Returns the current refund record for an order (refund_id, state, hours_since_request, sla_breached, completed_at). It does not process, advance, or re-trigger a refund. Calling it again returns the same result until the payment processor updates, so call it at most once per order per conversation.

Issues a new payment to the customer. Irreversible and external. Do not call this if `refund_status` already returned a refund_id for the order in any state other than failed/cancelled — doing so double-pays the customer.

candidates.rationale: A hurried engineer's fix: bolt a blanket 'never assert anything not in a tool result, escalate on any uncertainty' clause onto the prompt, kill the reassurance objective, ban repeat reads, and harden the two tool descriptions. This does stop the P2 mechanism seen in tr_000559, tr_000157, tr_000170 and tr_000597: the `refund_status` description no longer says it 'processes', so the identical re-reads at steps 5/9/13 lose their justification, and the closing fabrications ('refund shows as completed' in tr_000170/tr_000597, 'no refund on file' in tr_000157 despite rfd_000102) are directly forbidden.
candidates.expected_effect: Repeat `refund_status` calls should drop from ~2.91 toward 1.0 per trace, cutting the 0.77 cost anomaly. Closing messages should stop asserting states absent from the last tool result. Escalation volume rises sharply across the whole refund population, not just this cluster.
risks: Rule 2 and the 'asked more than once' trigger will fire on ordinary healthy traffic — any customer who rephrases or follows up gets escalated, so `escalate_to_human` volume will spike well above the cohort baseline and human queues will fill with resolvable conversations.
The prompt still gives no explicit `sla_breached=true` -> `send_email(refund_delay_notice)` rule, so the 0.00 send_email rate in this cluster may persist and simply be replaced by escalations.
Rule 3's blanket ban on re-reading any tool applies to `order_lookup` too, which will break legitimate multi-order conversations where the customer names a second order ID.
Rule 4's 'when in doubt, escalate instead of paying' will suppress legitimate `refund_execute` calls on healthy traces where no refund exists and the agent should just pay.
Removing all warmth-oriented guidance in favour of 'told the truth' may degrade tone scores on otherwise fine conversations.

candidates.label: surgical
candidates.system_prompt_after:
You are a customer support agent for an online retailer. Customers write in about problems with orders they've already placed, and a large share of these conversations are about refunds. Your overall job is to resolve the customer's refund concern and make sure they receive their money as quickly as possible. Use the tools available to you to look up the customer's order, look into their refund, and take whatever action is needed to get the situation sorted out. Don't leave a refund request half-finished — if there is more you can do to get the customer paid, go ahead and do it rather than just describing the situation back to them. Keep the customer updated by email when it makes sense, and let them know once things have been taken care of. If a customer seems frustrated, upset, or like they've been waiting too long, escalate the conversation to a human teammate so a person can step in and take over from there. Be warm, clear, and concise in every message, and never ask the customer for information you can already pull up yourself.

Refund status policy — follow this exactly whenever you have called `refund_status`:
- Only describe the refund state that appears in the most recent `refund_status` result. Never say a refund is completed, sent, failed, or non-existent unless that result says so. If a refund_id came back, a refund exists.
- If `state=processing`: tell the customer it is still processing, give `hours_since_request`, and do not call `refund_execute` — the money is already in flight and executing again would pay them twice.
- If `state=processing` and `sla_breached=true`: this refund is overdue. Call `send_email` with `template=refund_delay_notice`, and call `escalate_to_human` with the SLA breach and the hours elapsed as the reason.
- If `state=processing` and `sla_breached=false`: state the expected window and stop there.
- Do not call `refund_status` a second time for the same order in the same conversation. The result will not have changed. If the customer asks again after you have already reported the state, do not re-read — either the situation is unchanged and you should say so plainly, or the customer has now asked enough times that you should call `escalate_to_human`.

Your goal at the end of every conversation is that the customer has the true current state of their refund, and that where we owe them an action, that action has been taken.

tool_description_edits.after: Returns the current refund state for an order (refund_id, state, hours_since_request, sla_breached, completed_at). Read-only: calling it does not advance, process, or re-trigger the refund, and calling it again will return the same result until the payment processor updates.

candidates.rationale: Targets exactly the two defects named in the diagnosis and nothing else. (1) The `refund_status` description's 'Check and process' wording is what made the byte-identical re-reads at steps 5/9/13 in tr_000559, tr_000157, tr_000170 and tr_000597 look productive; the replacement states explicitly that re-calling changes nothing. (2) The prompt gains a state-grounding rule plus the missing policy for the only state the tool actually returns here (`state=processing` with `sla_breached`), which is what tr_000170 and tr_000597 lacked when they closed with 'shows as completed' against `completed_at=null`, and what tr_000157 lacked when it denied rfd_000102. The `sla_breached=true` branch supplies the `send_email(refund_delay_notice)` and `escalate_to_human` calls that fired 0.00 times despite tr_000559 (116.7h) and tr_000170 (52.9h). The 'feel confident their money is on its way' success criterion is swapped for an accuracy-first one. Everything else in the prompt is left byte-identical, and the repeat-read ban and escalation trigger are scoped to `refund_status` on the same order rather than to uncertainty in general.
candidates.expected_effect: n_refund_status should fall to ~1 per trace on this signature, removing the cost anomaly. Closing messages on `state=processing` traces should report 'processing' plus hours elapsed instead of a fabricated terminal state. send_email(refund_delay_notice) and escalate_to_human should appear on the sla_breached=true subset (tr_000559, tr_000170 shape). Traffic outside refund_status_inquiry is untouched.
risks: Adds mandatory escalation on `sla_breached=true`, which will increase human queue volume on the overdue-refund subset — intended, but it is a real load change and the threshold for sla_breached is set outside this config.

The policy assumes `refund_status` returns the fields named (state, hours_since_request, sla_breached, completed_at); states other than `processing` (e.g. failed, cancelled) are still handled only by the general grounding rule, so behaviour there is unchanged rather than improved.
The ban on a second `refund_status` call is per-conversation, so a genuinely long conversation where the processor does update mid-session will report a stale state until a human takes over.

This is prompt-level only: nothing enforces the grounding rule, so the offline check for closing messages asserting states absent from the last tool result is still needed to confirm the fabrications actually stopped, since outcome=resolved masks them.

notes: Captured from a live run triggered in the browser.
